title: Stephen Miller’s deportation machine, by the numbers: 3,000 a day was the order. Here is what it delivered
dek: Removals up by about half, a detention population that peaked at 70,766, 36 deaths in custody in one fiscal year, two U.S. citizens shot dead in Minneapolis, a department shut down, and six in ten voters saying it went too far. The ledger of the program the new chief of staff built.
body:
In May 2025, four months into the second term, Stephen Miller went on Fox News and gave the number that has organized American immigration enforcement ever since: the administration wanted “a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day” [1]. Axios reported that he and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem had set it as a quota; the Justice Department later told a court there was no quota [2]. He told the agency to arrest anyone in the country illegally, not only people with criminal records, and said it should look where day laborers gather, after which Home Depot parking lots became a regular site of arrests [3].

Eighteen months later the man who gave the order is chief of staff. The ledger of what the order produced is below, from the government’s own figures where they exist and from the researchers who count them where they do not.

## Arrests: the target was never reached

ICE’s intake of people into detention, the closest public measure of arrests, peaked at 1,053 a day in June 2025 [5]. In March 2026 it was 955 a day; adding Border Patrol’s transfers, about 1,049 people a day entered ICE custody [5]. ABC News reported in July that June 2026 was the busiest month of the year, with just over 43,000 arrests by ICE and Customs and Border Protection together, or 1,438 a day, and that the administration was now aiming for 2,000 [6]. The Migration Policy Institute counted more than 50,000 arrests a month in three consecutive months [7]. By every published count, the daily number has run at between a third and a half of the 3,000 Miller named.

## Removals: up by about half, short of the promise

The last full year of the Biden administration, fiscal 2024, ended with 271,484 removals by ICE [4]. Fiscal 2025, which the two administrations split, ended with 319,980 [5]. In fiscal 2026 the pace rose: 234,236 removals by April 4 [5], 356,389 by July 21 [6]. Kocher projected in April that the year would end above 460,000, which would pass the Obama administration’s record of 438,421 in fiscal 2013 [5][6]. Mike Howell, whose Trump-aligned Oversight Project sued for the raw numbers, was blunt about what that meant: “The numbers are only larger than Obama in absolute terms,” he said, adding that without worksite enforcement they would not reach “mass deportation levels” [6].

The administration counts more broadly. The Migration Policy Institute, in an October 22 estimate, put all deportations in fiscal 2026, removals and returns together, at about 660,000, against a stated goal of one million a year [7]. Of roughly 980,000 deportations between January 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, about 680,000 were people turned around at or near the border and about 300,000 were arrested inside the country [7]. The Department of Homeland Security has said more than 2.2 million people “self-deported,” a figure built on surveys; MPI’s Marc Rosenblum estimated between 310,000 and 1.5 million, and counted about 170,000 who took formal voluntary departure [7]. The administration has devoted about $240 billion to the program, by MPI’s accounting [7].

## Detention: a record 70,766, three-quarters of them without a conviction

The detained population, which stood at 59,762 in September 2025, reached 65,135 by November 16, 2025, and a record 70,766 on January 24, 2026 [4][5]. It was 60,311 on April 4 and about 60,000 in the spring, by NPR’s count [5][8]. Who was in those beds is the number that defined the politics. TRAC found that 73.6 percent of detainees in November 2025 had no criminal conviction, and that 97 percent of the net increase since September was people without one [4]. The Cato Institute, analyzing the first weeks of fiscal 2026, found 73 percent without a conviction and 5 percent with a violent one [5]. ICE’s own framing in July was that 60 percent of detainees had a criminal record, a broader category than conviction [6].

## Deaths: 36 in a year, the most on record

ICE’s death-reporting page lists 36 deaths in custody in fiscal 2026, from October 4, 2025, to August 23, 2026, against 24 in fiscal 2025 and 12 in fiscal 2024 [8]. NPR reported in April that the year had already passed the previous record of 28, set in 2004 [8]. Austin Kocher, who tracks the agency’s data, counted 47 deaths since January 2025 as of April, 16 of them in 2026 [5]. DHS attributed the rise to the size of the detained population and gave a custody death rate of 0.009 percent [8]. Acting ICE director Todd Lyons told a House hearing on April 16 that the agency held more people than at any time since its founding in 2003, and said, “No death is what we want” [8]. Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock wrote that ICE had issued interim death notices within 48 hours in only 15 of 49 deaths since January 2025 [8]. One of the 36, Geraldo Lunas Campos, died January 3 at Camp East Montana in El Paso; DHS called it medical distress, the county medical examiner ruled it a homicide, and the FBI opened an investigation [8].

## Minneapolis: two citizens dead, a department shut down, a secretary gone

On January 6, 2026, DHS announced its largest enforcement operation ever, sending about 2,000 agents to Minneapolis and St. Paul [9]. The next morning an ICE agent, Jonathan Ross, shot Renée Good, a 37-year-old writer and U.S. citizen, three times through the window of her SUV as it moved away from him [9]. DHS called her actions “domestic terrorism”; Noem said, without evidence, that Good had been “stalking and impeding ICE all day”; Vice President JD Vance called her death “a tragedy of her own making” [9]. The Justice Department declined to open a civil rights investigation, and federal prosecutors in Minnesota and Washington and an FBI supervisor resigned in protest [9].

On January 24, two Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive-care nurse at the Minneapolis VA hospital, who had been filming agents and had a permit to carry a handgun [10]. Within hours Miller called him a “domestic terrorist” who had “tried to assassinate federal law enforcement” [10]. Video reviewed by Reuters and other outlets showed him holding a phone, not a gun, and agents firing about ten shots in five seconds, some after he was motionless [10][3]. Trump said days later that he did not believe Pretti had meant to assassinate anyone; the Justice Department opened a civil rights investigation on January 30; the Hennepin County medical examiner ruled the death a homicide [10]. Miller later said the agents “may not have been following” protocol [3]. Republican senators Bill Cassidy and Thom Tillis called for investigations, and the National Rifle Association and Gun Owners of America condemned officials who suggested that carrying a gun justified the shooting [10].

The consequences were institutional. Democrats refused to fund DHS without new limits on federal agents, and the department shut down on February 14; TSA lines grew and more than 400 screeners quit [11]. Trump removed Noem in early March. The Senate confirmed Sen. Markwayne Mullin to replace her on March 23, 54 to 45; at his hearing he said agents would generally need a judicial warrant to enter homes and businesses, and that he regretted calling Pretti a “deranged individual” [11]. Sen. Martin Heinrich, voting yes, said he looked forward to a secretary who did not take orders from Stephen Miller [11].

## The courts

The Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship 6-3 on June 30, striking down the executive order Trump signed in January 2025; Miller called the decision “destructive and outrageous” and announced a ban on “birth tourism” instead [12][3]. In October the Labor Department suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms from the PERM green card labor program, a decision the AP says Miller helped lead [13][14]. And on the list of actions Miller and budget director Russell Vought drew up for a Democratic Congress, Reuters reported, are tighter rules on visas for foreign students and temporary workers [15].

## The voters

Tuesday’s electorate rendered the only verdict that counts in the near term. In the AP Voter Poll, about six in ten voters said the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far, about two in ten said not far enough, and about two in ten said it was about right [16]. CNN’s exit poll had Democrats winning Latino voters by 30 points [17]. A YouGov poll in the week after Good’s death had found 46 percent of Americans in favor of abolishing ICE and 43 percent opposed [9]. The man whose program they were judging now runs the White House, and the chairman of the committee that will investigate it has told him to lawyer up [14].
